title: 1 Samuel 14:47–52
context: 1 Samuel 14:47–52 is a summary of Saul’s reign. It lists his campaigns against Moab, Ammon, Edom, the kings of Zobah, the Philistines and the Amalekites, his family members and the commander of his army, Abner. The summary acknowledges Saul’s real achievements: he fought valiantly and delivered Israel from plunderers. It closes by noting the continual war with the Philistines and Saul’s practice of recruiting mighty men. Such summaries often close a section of a king’s story; here it prepares for chapter 15, where Saul’s rejection is confirmed.

verses.text: Now when Saul had taken the kingdom over Israel, he fought against all his enemies on every side: against Moab, and against the children of Ammon, and against Edom, and against the kings of Zobah, and against the Philistines. Wherever he turned himself, he defeated them.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul fights “against all his enemies on every side,” and the narrator adds, “Wherever he turned himself, he defeated them.” Arminian readers note that the narrative honestly acknowledges Saul’s real successes. God used Saul to protect Israel, even after the rebuke of 13:13–14.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Saul’s victories fulfill in part the purpose for which he was anointed, to save Israel from its enemies (9:16). God’s purposes continue through a flawed king. Shared ground: both traditions read the summary as a fair acknowledgment of Saul’s achievements, alongside the narrative’s account of his failures.

verses.text: He did valiantly and struck the Amalekites, and delivered Israel out of the hands of those who plundered them.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul “did valiantly and struck the Amalekites, and delivered Israel out of the hands of those who plundered them.” Arminian readers note the positive evaluation. Saul’s courage and service to Israel are real and deserve recognition.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the mention of the Amalekites prepares for chapter 15, where Saul’s incomplete obedience regarding Amalek leads to his final rejection. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as recognizing Saul’s genuine service, while seeing it as a bridge to the following narrative.

verses.text: Now the sons of Saul were Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua; and the names of his two daughters were these: the name of the firstborn Merab, and the name of the younger Michal.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul’s sons are Jonathan, Ishvi and Malchishua, and his daughters Merab and Michal. Arminian readers note that the family list introduces figures who will matter later, especially Jonathan and Michal in their relationships with David (18:20).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that other lists name Abinadab (31:2) and Eshbaal (1 Chronicles 8:33) among Saul’s sons; this passage does not explain the relationship between the lists. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as background, and both caution against speculation about the differences between the family lists.

verses.text: The name of Saul’s wife was Ahinoam the daughter of Ahimaaz. The name of the captain of his army was Abner the son of Ner, Saul’s uncle.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul’s wife is Ahinoam the daughter of Ahimaaz, and his army commander is Abner the son of Ner, Saul’s uncle. Arminian readers note that Abner will play a major role in later events, including the struggle over the kingdom after Saul’s death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the list of Saul’s household shows the beginnings of a royal court and administration. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical background, introducing characters who will matter later in the story, and neither finds a theological dispute in it.

verses.text: Kish was the father of Saul, and Ner the father of Abner was the son of Abiel.
verses.arminianNotes: “Kish was the father of Saul, and Ner the father of Abner was the son of Abiel.” Arminian readers note that the genealogy ties Saul and Abner together as close kin, which helps explain Abner’s loyalty to Saul’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the genealogical precision, which grounds the narrative in real family history. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a simple genealogical note, and neither draws theological conclusions from it.

verses.text: There was severe war against the Philistines all the days of Saul; and when Saul saw any mighty man or any valiant man, he took him into his service.
verses.arminianNotes: “There was severe war against the Philistines all the days of Saul,” and Saul recruited every mighty and valiant man he saw. Arminian readers note that the Philistine threat was never fully removed in Saul’s reign. The summary ends on a note of continuing struggle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Saul’s practice of conscripting warriors fulfills Samuel’s warning about kings (8:11), though the narrative does not dwell on it here. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a realistic close to the summary, showing a reign marked by ongoing conflict and preparing for chapter 15.
